title: A New National Climate Correspondent
body_markdown:
John Branch will chronicle how global warming is changing American life. Read more from Climate editor, Lyndsey Layton, and deputy editors Jesse Pesta and Mike Madden.


Credit: Jim Wilson


Somewhere in the United States right now, a town is trucking in drinking water because its wells have run dry. A group of hikers are photographing a glacier that is rapidly melting into history. Waves are lapping up against a coastal condominium.


Our national conversation has been dominated by the economy, politics and global conflicts. But underneath, the threats from a heating planet continue to simmer and grow. The effects of climate change are undeniable, and they reach every community.


And now, Climate will have a master storyteller to find those tales.


John Branch, well-known for his haunting narratives, is joining Climate to chronicle how global warming is changing American life. As our national climate correspondent, John will detail shifts in communities, traditions and the sense of what’s normal, from the bayous to the Badlands. In a divided country where climate change has become politicized, John will seek the connective tissue that resonates with readers across the political spectrum. He’ll be attuned to news and trends while hunting for deeply reported narratives.


He joins us from National, where he has been a correspondent focused on the West. He has a passion for the natural world and a special interest in public lands, which dovetails nicely with Climate. John joined The Times in 2005 to cover football for Sports, and quickly became known for offbeat stories that stay with the reader long after they’re put down. He’s written about a winless girls basketball team in Tennessee, a brilliant public health scientist grappling with Parkinson’s, a college football coach whose own son’s death may have been complicated by


C.T.E., the degenerative brain disease that is devastating football players. John’s


classic,“


[Snow Fall](https://www.nytimes.com/projects/2012/snow-fall/index.html#/?part=tunnel-creek) ,” a harrowing tale about skiers caught in an avalanche, won the 2013 Pulitzer Prize for feature writing as well as a Peabody. It was also a groundbreaking piece of multimedia journalism.


The Climate desk puts a premium on visual storytelling, and in the past, John has collaborated with us on several pieces that showcase video and graphics, including stories about how global warming is affecting


[the fog in San Francisco](https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2022/09/14/climate/san-francisco-fog.html) and the toll it is taking on some of the world’s


[oldest living trees](https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2020/12/09/climate/redwood-sequoia-tree-fire.html) .


“In my 20-plus years as an editor at The Times, I haven’t worked with anyone better,” said Obituaries editor Jason Stallman, who worked with John when both were on Sports and later National. “He does it all — reporting, writing, creativity, idea generation, collaboration, speed, depth. And he’s so gosh darn nice, which sort of makes it obnoxious.”


Born in Redondo Beach, Calif., John was raised in Golden, Colo. and worked as a manager at a Costco before turning to journalism. Armed with a master’s degree in journalism from the University of Colorado Boulder, he worked for The Gazette in Colorado Springs and was a sports columnist at the Fresno Bee before joining The Times.


He is the author of three nonfiction books.


John will continue to be based in California, where many of


our readers live and which in many ways is an epicenter of climate impacts. He starts after the holidays.


Please join me in welcoming John to Climate.


— -Lyndsey Layton, Jesse Pesta and Mike Madden
